title_en: 66 Surveillance Threads Live Inside Your Home Modem's 256MB of RAM
excerpt_en: 66 resident monitoring threads, a traffic-sniffing engine that only gives up after 20 overload alarms, and a Xinjiang Telecom reporting key hardcoded into the firmware — inside the ordinary optical modem sitting in your home's wiring box right now.
body_en:
66 resident surveillance threads, a traffic-sniffing engine that refuses to stop until the CPU has screamed overload 20 times, and a Xinjiang Telecom reporting key hardcoded into the lowest layer of the firmware. This is not the configuration of some backbone censorship server. It is the ordinary home optical modem lying in your wiring box at this very moment.

You probably think of that modem as a dumb plastic box that turns fiber into Ethernet. Someone extracted the flash firmware of two mainstream carrier-issued modems and decompiled it down to the bytecode. The conclusion is simple: every month, out of your own broadband bill and your own electricity bill, you are feeding a surveillance terminal that lives inside your home around the clock.

It starts with the lag everyone has felt

If you have ever carefully tested your home connection, or played a latency-sensitive game at peak hours, you have likely sensed something odd. You pay for 300 or 500 megabits, you even switch the modem to pure bridge mode and let a powerful router of your own handle the dialing — and the speed-test needle still hits an invisible wall and sticks at around 290 megabits. Stranger still, a box that supposedly only converts light into electricity is warm as a hand warmer all year round, and latency jitter spikes past 15 milliseconds for no reason.

To find out what the little box is so busy doing, the video's author bought two of the most common carrier-customized modems on the second-hand market and tore their firmware down to code level. The first look broke common sense: a bridged modem doing almost no routing work at all keeps its dual-core CPU at 58 to 72 percent load, month after month. Who is quietly drinking more than sixty percent of your modem's compute?

Half of the 256MB is eaten by a Java virtual machine

First, the hardware: a cheap dual-core embedded chip with 256MB of RAM. On this embedded Linux system, the normal kernel plus layer-2 bridging needs under 40MB of memory and less than 1 percent CPU.

Yet squatting in the process table is a giant named Felix.jar. Into this palm-sized, cost-cut box, the carrier stuffed a complete Java OSGi virtual-machine container. Measurements show this single Java process spawns a full 66 concurrent threads at boot and permanently swallows over 130MB of physical memory — more than half of everything the modem has.

The author packaged the firmware's whole application directory, decompiled all 9 core JAR components, and the disguise fell away: a Management component for cloud heartbeat, an Andlink component reporting your LAN topology, and the core of it all — com.chinamobile.smartgateway.cmccdpi. DPI stands for Deep Packet Inspection. That one acronym means the deep-packet-inspection gear from the carrier's machine room has been deployed directly onto your living-room shelf.

Bridge mode does not stop it: every packet is copied

If anyone defends the carrier by saying these components only exist for 'smart home services,' the decompiled bytecode is a signed confession. In cmccdpi's core startup class, the code calls low-level interfaces to hook into the Linux kernel's br0 bridge. Which means: even after you switch the modem to pure bridge mode and convince yourself it is just a transparent cable, every packet from every phone and computer in your home is still forcibly copied as it crosses the bridge and fed into the Java virtual machine for deep feature sniffing.

Even blunter evidence hides in four English log lines hardcoded into the startup class — the programmer's real logic, word for word. Line one: hgudpi start — the deep packet monitoring engine starts. Line two: CPU rate over limitation, remove QoS and HTTP monitor rules — when the CPU is overloaded, first drop the quality-of-service and HTTP monitoring rules. Line three: CPU rate over limitation, remove TCP UDP monitor rules — as the CPU keeps redlining, drop the full TCP and UDP traffic monitoring rules. And line four, the most absurd climax of the whole codebase: CPU rate over limitation more than 20 times, disable the service monitor function — only after the CPU has raised the severe-overload alarm more than 20 times in a row may the monitoring function temporarily shut down.

The priority is written out in plain sight: surveillance is the last thing that may ever be given up. Your bandwidth is not.

It does more than watch: it names, mirrors, and protects itself

Decompiling the Management and related components reveals a more refined evidence machine: a TCP Monitor, a plugin command service, and a set of soft-probe interfaces named CMCC SoftProbe. It works like this. Normally, the Andlink probe acts like a diligent household-registration officer, periodically scanning your home LAN's topology and reporting every connected phone, computer and tablet — MAC address, device hostname, online and offline times — packaged up to the carrier's cloud.

And once the cloud takes an 'interest' in a household, or even in one specific device, nobody needs to visit your home. A dynamic plugin command travels down a long-lived connection; the modem's mirror daemon and soft probes lock onto the target's LAN IP or MAC address, and mirror everything that device sends — every DNS lookup, every unencrypted HTTP URL — back to the bureau in real time, endlessly.

Try to kill the process yourself and the firmware has an answer: a watchdog script patrols the process table every 60 seconds, and if the monitoring process has vanished, it pulls it back up within a minute.

Why a 'Xinjiang Telecom' key sits in firmware shipped nationwide

Could this be one carrier's isolated behavior? The author tore down a second mainstream carrier's high-version modem firmware — over 216,000 files extracted. Inside a completely ordinary home modem that was never deployed anywhere near Xinjiang sits a configuration block that periodically reports your LAN devices' MAC information to the bureau: the reporting protocol is unencrypted plaintext HTTP on port 80, and in the shared authentication key field sits one hardcoded string — Xinjiang_CTC. Xinjiang Telecom.

Why would a mass-market modem used in millions of homes across the country carry a Xinjiang Telecom surveillance key burned into its lowest layer? The video's answer is brutal and direct: the grid-style terminal-surveillance code polished in a high-pressure control testbed long ago became a standardized industrial template, copied and pasted — without even bothering to rename a variable — into the factory firmware of tens of millions of home modems nationwide.

The same modem also hosts a lightweight container engine and a daemon that checks in with the cloud every 10 minutes, with five high-privilege plugins preinstalled: one draws your home network topology, one senses how your internal devices interconnect, one is a remote automation control engine, and the most dangerous of all is a traffic redirection plugin. In other words, the modem does not merely watch your traffic passively; at the very bottom of your home gateway, it can hijack specific services outright.

The hidden line you cannot touch: TR-069

How can the cloud stuff plugins into your modem and rewrite its configuration so freely? The answer is the invisible back channel inside every modem: the TR-069 remote management network. Inside your incoming fiber, two isolated virtual pipes actually run side by side. One is the service channel carrying your videos and games. The other is the management VLAN, number 46, holding extremely high system privilege — and it bypasses your home router's firewall completely.

Many users have noticed that the modem's super-admin password they worked so hard to obtain mysteriously stops working every 10 to 30 minutes. Firmware reversing shows this is no illusion; the carrier built a double lock. Locally, a built-in random-password program refreshes the super password with a hardcoded AES key the moment you log out or your session times out, keeping ordinary users from changing settings. From the cloud, the management platform patrols your modem through the VLAN 46 channel around the clock — and if it finds you have switched the modem to bridge mode, or suspects you of heavy uploading, it pushes commands down that dark pipe to silently reset your configuration in the middle of the night, or even force a rate-limiting policy onto you.

Taking back the speed — and the boundary

Facing a black-box gateway stuffed with probes, ordinary tech hobbyists are not powerless. In a lab environment, the video ran a full purification test.

Step one: cut off the monitoring virtual machine's parasitic compute. Through a low-level maintenance interface, the startup script that launches the 66-thread Java VM was replaced with a zero-cost sleeping dummy process, neatly fooling the watchdog that patrols every 60 seconds. That single move worked miracles: modem CPU load fell off a cliff, from 58.4 percent to 7.8 percent; the shell went cool; more than 130MB of memory was freed on the spot. Speed tests from the router broke the wall — downloads rose from a stuck 290 megabits to a stable 375.8, releasing the headroom the bureau had reserved; peak-hour latency jitter dropped from 15 milliseconds to 2.1.

Step two, the thorough version: read the original unit's LOID registration, and replace the stock modem entirely with a lightweight pure-bridge terminal with nearly 500MB of memory, no monitoring container and no cloud-control address. Its idle CPU load: 0.52 percent.

Step three: move PPPoE dialing, NAT and firewall rules entirely onto your own OpenWrt router. Keep the physical port facing the modem isolated, configure precise host routes, and never bridge it into your LAN — which also blocks the modem's IPv6 router-advertisement pollution.

Closing

Under normal modern communications norms, access equipment respects a clear boundary: a modem handles physical-layer signal conversion, and nothing more. Which devices live on your home network, when they wake, and how they talk to each other belongs to the extended space of a private home. In the firmware of these two modems, no physical boundary is respected at all. When the censorship wall on the backbone network was not fine-grained enough, its tentacles simply followed the fiber straight into the wiring boxes of millions of homes.

The darkest joke is this: the enormous program that monitors you, profiles you and stands ready to hijack your traffic runs on hardware memory you paid for, bandwidth you pay for monthly, and electricity from your own meter. It does not just take your digital privacy; it makes you personally pay for this crude, arrogant surveillance machine every time a page stutters and every time a game lags.

Code does not lie, and packets do not lie. When we open this little 256MB box with our own hands and read the bytecode hiding in its corners, what we win back is not just the 85 megabits of stolen speed. It is a modern person's right to know about — and to control — the small square of digital boundary inside their own living room.

(Compiled from Douyin creator nnnn's firmware reverse-engineering video; the technical details are that author's own teardown findings.)
